the provider has failed to discharge its obligations under section 62F to the student by the end of the provider obligation period; and
either:
the Director decides, under paragraph 62J(2)(b), that the Director is not satisfied that there is a suitable replacement course for the student; or
the student elects, under subparagraph 62J(4)(a)(iii), to have an amount equal to the amount the provider was liable to pay the student under subsection 62F(8) paid to them.
Despite subsection (2), the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director is not required to pay an amount under that subsection if:
the Director becomes aware of the circumstances referred to in paragraph (2)(a) more than 12 months after the day the provider defaulted in relation to the student; or
the Director becomes aware of the circumstances referred to in subparagraph (2)(b)(ii) more than 12 months after the day the Director gives notice to the student under subsection 62J(4).

Despite subsection (1), the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director may pay a greater amount than the amount required to be paid under that subsection to the provider of the replacement course if the Director considers that to do so:
would best protect the interests of the student; and
would not jeopardise the sustainability of the Higher Education Tuition Protection Fund.
Despite subsection (1), if:
the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director is required under that subsection to pay an amount to the provider of the replacement course; and
the amount required to be paid is more than the cost of the replacement course;
the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director must pay the difference to the student.
A payment under this section must be made in accordance with any requirements prescribed by the Up-front Payments Guidelines.

section.heading: Consequences of payments being made from the Higher Education Tuition Protection Fund

content.p: Cessation of claim
If:
a registered higher education provider defaults in relation to a domestic student; and
the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director pays an amount in accordance with section 62K in relation to the student;
the student ceases to have any claim against the provider in respect of the up-front payments made for the affected unit.
Provider must pay back Higher Education Tuition Protection Director

Instead, the provider must pay the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director an amount equal to the amount that the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director paid in relation to the student under section 62K.

The Higher Education Tuition Protection Director may, on behalf of the Commonwealth, recover that amount from the provider as a debt due to the Commonwealth by action in a court of competent jurisdiction.
Higher Education Tuition Protection Director may enforce security

If the provider had granted the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director a charge or other security over any of its assets, the Director may enforce the charge or security in satisfaction, or partial satisfaction, of the debt.

section.heading: Notification obligations for payments made from the Higher Education Tuition Protection Fund

content.p: This section applies if:
a registered higher education provider defaults in relation to a domestic student; and
the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director makes a payment to the registered higher education provider who provides the replacement course, or to the student, under section 62K.
The Higher Education Tuition Protection Director must give a written notice to the defaulting provider stating the amounts of any such payments.
Subdivision C—Obligations on replacement providers

section.heading: Obligations of providers to provide information about replacement courses

content.p: The Higher Education Tuition Protection Director may, by written notice, require a registered higher education provider to provide such information that the Director reasonably requires to enable the Director to make a decision under subsection 62J(2) regarding suitable replacement courses for a domestic student in relation to whom a provider has defaulted.
The information must be provided:
in a form (if any) approved by the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director for the information; and
in accordance with such other requirements as the Director makes.
Civil penalty
A registered higher education provider is liable to a civil penalty if:
the provider is given a notice under subsection (1); and
the provider fails to comply with the notice.
Civil penalty: 60 penalty units.
Offence
A registered higher education provider commits an offence of strict liability if:
the provider is given a notice under subsection (1); and
the provider fails to comply with the notice.
Penalty: 60 penalty units.
This section applies if a domestic student accepts an offer of a place in a replacement unit or replacement course as referred to in paragraph 62F(3)(a) or subsection 62J(5).

The registered higher education provider who provides the replacement course or replacement unit must give written notice of the acceptance to the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director within 14 days of the acceptance.
The registered higher education provider who provides the replacement unit or replacement course must ensure that the student:
(a) for a replacement course—is granted credits for units of study of the original course successfully completed by the student; and
if the student has paid tuition fees for an affected unit of the original course—is not charged tuition fees for the replacement unit or the replacement unit of the replacement course; and
is enrolled in the replacement unit or replacement course as soon as practicable.
Civil penalty
A registered higher education provider is liable to a civil penalty if the provider contravenes this section.
Civil penalty: 60 penalty units.
Offence
A registered higher education provider commits an offence of strict liability if the provider contravenes this section.
Penalty: 60 penalty units.

section.heading: Obligations of replacement providers regarding enrolment information

content.p: A registered higher education provider who provides a replacement unit or replacement course to a domestic student must keep up to date records of the following in relation to the student:
the student’s full name and contact details;
the name of the replacement unit or the replacement course (and units of study) that the student is currently enrolled in;
any tuition fees paid (or incurred) by the student for the replacement unit or for any units of study of the replacement course;
any payments made by the Director under section 62K to the provider in relation to the replacement course;
details of the replacement unit or units of study of the replacement course successfully completed by the student;
details of the credits granted to the student for the replacement unit or for the units of study of the original course successfully completed by the student.
Civil penalty
A registered higher education provider is liable to a civil penalty if the provider contravenes this section.
Civil penalty: 60 penalty units.
Offence
A registered higher education provider commits an offence of strict liability if the provider contravenes this section.
Penalty: 60 penalty units.
Subdivision D—Miscellaneous

(1) If a registered higher education provider (the original provider) for a unit of study or an Australian course of study enters into an arrangement with one or more other registered higher education providers to provide the unit or course jointly to one or more domestic students, the arrangement must:
be such that the students pay their tuition fees directly to the original provider; or
both:
be in writing; and
provide for the receipt and disbursement of any tuition fees paid by students directly to any of the other providers.

However, for the purpose of determining the original provider’s obligations under the tuition protection requirements, any tuition fees paid by students directly to any of the other providers are taken to have been paid directly to the original provider.
Civil penalty
A registered higher education provider is liable to a civil penalty if the provider contravenes subsection (1).
Civil penalty: 60 penalty units.
Offence
A registered higher education provider commits an offence of strict liability if the provider contravenes subsection (1).
Penalty: 60 penalty units.

section.heading: Other tuition protection information must be provided

content.p: This section applies to a registered higher education provider if:
the Higher Education Tuition Protection Director believes on reasonable grounds that the provider has information relevant to the Director’s functions under this Act; and
the Director, by written notice given to the provider, requests the provider to give the Director the information:
within the period (not shorter than 14 days after the notice is given) specified in the notice; and
in the manner specified in the notice.
The provider must comply with the notice within the period specified in the notice.
Civil penalty
A registered higher education provider is liable to a civil penalty if the provider contravenes subsection (2).
Civil penalty: 60 penalty units.
Offence
A registered higher education provider commits an offence of strict liability if the provider contravenes subsection (2).
Penalty: 60 penalty units.

section.heading: Right to refund may be cancelled etc. without compensation

content.p: A right to be paid an amount under section 62K is granted on the basis that:
the right may be cancelled, revoked, terminated or varied by or under later legislation; and
no compensation is payable if the right is so cancelled, revoked, terminated or varied.

section.heading: Continuing application of Part to certain persons

content.p: This Part continues to apply in relation to a person that was a registered higher education provider as if the person were still a registered higher education provider.
Subsection (1) applies for the purposes of dealing with or resolving any matter that arose during, or that relates to, the period when the person was a registered higher education provider.

division.heading: Requiring people to give information etc.

section.heading: Requiring certain persons to give information etc.

content.p: This section applies to a person if TEQSA believes on reasonable grounds that:
the person is, or was, connected with:
a regulated entity; or
a former regulated entity; and
the person is capable of giving or producing information, a document or a thing relevant to TEQSA’s function in paragraph 134(1)(c) (about investigating compliance with this Act).

This section also applies to a person if TEQSA believes on reasonable grounds that the person is capable of giving or producing information, or a document or a thing, relating to a matter that constitutes, or may constitute, a contravention of section 114A or 114B.
TEQSA may, by written notice given to the person, require the person:
to give TEQSA the information; or
to produce to TEQSA the document or thing; or
to make copies of the document and to produce to TEQSA those copies;
within the period and in the manner specified in the notice.
The notice must:
not specify a period shorter than 14 days after the notice is given, unless TEQSA reasonably considers that a shorter period is necessary that is at least 24 hours after the notice is given; and
set out the effect of section 64.
Subsection (1) does not apply to:
a lawyer who is acting, or has acted, for the regulated entity or former regulated entity; or
national security information; or
documents or things relating to national security.
Subsection (1A) does not apply to:
a lawyer who is acting, or has acted, for a person who is suspected of contravening, or has contravened, section 114A or 114B; or
national security information; or
documents or things relating to national security.

section.heading: Contravening requirement to give information etc.

content.p: A person commits an offence if:
the person has been given a notice under subsection 63(2); and
the person fails to comply with a requirement in the notice.
Penalty: 30 penalty units.
A person is entitled to be paid by TEQSA, on behalf of the Commonwealth, reasonable compensation for complying with a requirement covered by paragraph 63(2)(c).

section.heading: TEQSA may retain documents and things

content.p: TEQSA may retain documents and things etc.
If a document (including a copy of a document), or a thing, is produced to TEQSA under section 63, TEQSA:
may take possession of, and may make copies of, the document or thing; and
may retain possession of the document or thing for such period as is necessary:
for the purposes of this Act; or
for the purposes of an investigation to which the document or thing relates; or
to enable evidence to be secured for the purposes of a prosecution or civil penalty proceeding.
Access and certified copy to be provided
Subsections (3) to (5) apply to a document produced under paragraph 63(2)(b).
The person otherwise entitled to possession of the document is entitled to be supplied, as soon as practicable, with a copy certified by TEQSA to be a true copy.
The certified copy must be received in all courts and tribunals as evidence as if it were the original.

Until a certified copy is supplied, TEQSA must, at such times and places as TEQSA thinks appropriate, permit the person otherwise entitled to possession of the document, or a person authorised by that person, to inspect and make copies of, or take extracts from, the document.
If:
a document (other than a copy of a document), or thing, is produced to TEQSA under section 63; and
TEQSA can no longer retain it under paragraph 66(1)(b);
TEQSA must take reasonable steps to return it, unless the document or thing is forfeited or forfeitable to the Commonwealth or is the subject of a dispute as to ownership.
The document or thing must be returned to the person who produced it (or to the owner if that person is not entitled to possess it).
TEQSA may dispose of a document or thing in such manner as it considers appropriate if:
the document or thing is produced to TEQSA under section 63; and
under section 67, TEQSA is required to take reasonable steps to return the document or thing to a person; and
either:
TEQSA cannot, despite making reasonable efforts, locate the person; or
the person has refused to take possession of the document or thing.

If the operation of this section would result in an acquisition of property from a person otherwise than on just terms, the Commonwealth is liable to pay a reasonable amount of compensation to the person.

If the Commonwealth and the person do not agree on the amount of the compensation, the person may institute proceedings in the Federal Court for the recovery from the Commonwealth of such reasonable amount of compensation as the court determines.
A person is not excused from:
giving information; or
producing a document (including a copy of a document) or thing;
under section 63 on the ground that doing so might tend to incriminate the person or expose the person to a penalty.
However, in the case of an individual, none of the following:
the information given;
the document, copy or thing produced;
the giving of the information or the producing of the document, copy or thing;
any information, document or thing obtained as a direct or indirect consequence of giving the information or producing the document, copy or thing;
is admissible in evidence against the individual:
in civil proceedings for the recovery of a penalty; or
in criminal proceedings, other than proceedings for an offence against:
section 64; or
(ii) section 137.1 or 137.2 of the Criminal Code (which deals with false or misleading information or documents) that relates to this Act; or
(iii) section 149.1 of the Criminal Code (which deals with obstruction of Commonwealth public officials) that relates to this Act.
(1) TEQSA may, in writing, appoint a member of the staff of TEQSA as an authorised officer for the purposes of this Act.
TEQSA must not appoint a person as an authorised officer unless:
the person holds the classification of APS Executive Level 1 or higher, or an equivalent classification; and
TEQSA is satisfied that the person has suitable qualifications and experience to properly exercise the powers of an authorised officer.
An authorised officer must, in exercising powers as an authorised officer, comply with any directions of TEQSA.
If a direction is given under subsection (3) in writing, the direction is not a legislative instrument.
• There are administrative sanctions for non-compliant registered higher education providers.
• There are a range of offences and civil penalties for contraventions of this Act.
• The Regulatory Powers Act is triggered to allow a range of enforcement actions in relation to this Act.

• Authorised officers are permitted to enter premises under a monitoring warrant or with consent of the occupier and to exercise monitoring powers under that Act for the purposes of determining whether various provisions of this Act or instruments under this Act have been complied with.

• Authorised officers may enter premises and exercise investigation powers to determine whether there has been a contravention of provisions of this Act or an offence against the Crimes Act 1914 or the Criminal Code that relates to this Act.
• A relevant court can order the payment of a civil penalty for a contravention of a civil penalty provision.
• Infringement notices can be issued for an alleged contravention of a civil penalty provision.
• Undertakings to comply with this Act may be accepted and enforced under the Regulatory Powers Act. If a person gives an undertaking, the undertaking may be enforced by a court order.

• A court can grant an injunction restraining a person from contravening a provision of this Act or requiring a person to comply with a provision of this Act. A court can also grant an injunction relating to online locations that facilitate provision of, or advertising of, academic cheating services.
Subdivision A—Sanctions
This Subdivision applies if a registered higher education provider has:
failed to meet the Threshold Standards; or
breached a condition imposed on its registration; or
breached a condition imposed on its authorisation as an authorised offshore provider; or
breached a condition imposed on the accreditation of a course of study accredited in relation to the provider; or
failed to ensure that an accredited course in relation to the provider meets the Threshold Standards;
or if circumstances exist in relation to the provider that are of a kind specified in regulations made for the purposes of this section.
Note: TEQSA may impose conditions under section 32, 44J or 53 instead of, or in addition to, applying a sanction under this Subdivision.
For a failure or breach relating to a course of study, TEQSA may:
shorten the period of accreditation of the course of study; or
cancel the accreditation of the course of study.
TEQSA may shorten the period of the provider’s registration.
TEQSA may cancel the provider’s registration.
However, before doing so, TEQSA must give the provider and the Minister for each relevant State and Territory responsible for higher education:
a written notice stating that TEQSA intends to make a decision to cancel the provider’s registration for specified reasons; and
a reasonable opportunity to make representations to TEQSA in relation to the proposed decision.
TEQSA must have regard to any representations received under subsection (2).
Subsection (2) does not apply if TEQSA is satisfied that the circumstances require immediate action.
TEQSA may cancel the provider’s authorisation as an authorised offshore provider.
However, before doing so, TEQSA must give the provider:
a written notice stating that TEQSA intends to make a decision to cancel the provider’s authorisation for specified reasons; and
a reasonable opportunity to make representations to TEQSA in relation to the proposed decision.
TEQSA must have regard to any representations received under subsection (2).

section.heading: TEQSA to notify provider of decision to impose sanction

content.p: TEQSA must, within 30 days after making a decision under section 99, 100, 101 or 101AA, notify the provider, in writing, of:
the decision; and
the reasons for the decision.
Subdivision B—Other matters

section.heading: Automatic cancellation if provider wound up

content.p: A registered higher education provider’s registration is cancelled, by force of this section, if a winding-up order is made in respect of the provider.
An entity whose registration under Part 3 is cancelled cannot reapply for registration for:
2 years after the cancellation takes effect; or
such shorter period as TEQSA considers appropriate.
An entity whose authorisation under Part 3A is cancelled cannot reapply for authorisation for:
2 years after the cancellation takes effect; or
such shorter period as TEQSA considers appropriate.
Note: There are offence and civil penalty provisions in Part 5A also.

section.heading: Offering a regulated higher education award if unregistered

content.p: Offence
A higher education provider commits an offence if the higher education provider is not a registered higher education provider.
Penalty: 300 penalty units.
Civil penalty
A higher education provider contravenes this subsection if the higher education provider is not a registered higher education provider.
Civil penalty: 600 penalty units.

section.heading: Representing offer of a regulated higher education award if unregistered

content.p: Offence
A regulated entity commits an offence if:
the entity represents that the entity:
is offering, or will offer, a regulated higher education award; or
is conferring, or will confer, a regulated higher education award; and
the entity is not a registered higher education provider.
Penalty: 300 penalty units.
Civil penalty
A regulated entity contravenes this subsection if:
the entity represents that the entity:
is offering, or will offer, a regulated higher education award; or
is conferring, or will confer, a regulated higher education award; and
the entity is not a registered higher education provider.
Civil penalty: 600 penalty units.

section.heading: Offering a regulated higher education award offshore if not authorised

content.p: Offence
A higher education provider commits an offence if:
the higher education provider offers or confers an Australian higher education award for the completion of an Australian course of study; and
the course of study is an offshore provided Australian course of study; and
the higher education provider is not an authorised offshore provider.
Penalty: 120 penalty units.
Civil penalty
A higher education provider contravenes this subsection if:
the higher education provider offers or confers an Australian higher education award for the completion of an Australian course of study; and
the course of study is an offshore provided Australian course of study; and
the higher education provider is not an authorised offshore provider.
Civil penalty: 240 penalty units.

section.heading: Offering an award without a course of study

content.p: Offence
A regulated entity commits an offence if:
the entity offers or confers:
an Australian higher education award; or
an overseas higher education award for the completion of a course of study provided wholly or mainly from Australian premises related to the award; and
for one or more students, the entity offers or confers the award:
without requiring the completion of a course of study; and
not as an honorary award.
Penalty: 300 penalty units.
Civil penalty
A regulated entity contravenes this subsection if:
the entity offers or confers:
an Australian higher education award; or
an overseas higher education award for the completion of a course of study provided wholly or mainly from Australian premises related to the award; and
for one or more students, the entity offers or confers the award:
without requiring the completion of a course of study; and
not as an honorary award.
Civil penalty: 600 penalty units.

section.heading: Regulated entity represents itself as university

content.p: Offence
A regulated entity commits an offence if:
the entity uses the word “university” to represent itself, or its operations, as a university in relation to:
an Australian course of study; or
an overseas course of study, to the extent that the course of study is, or is to be, provided wholly or mainly from Australian premises that are related to an overseas higher education award; or
a regulated higher education award; and
the entity is not a registered higher education provider registered in either the “Australian University” or “Overseas University” provider category.
Penalty: 300 penalty units.
Civil penalty
A regulated entity contravenes this subsection if:
the entity uses the word “university” to represent itself, or its operations, as a university in relation to:
an Australian course of study; or
an overseas course of study, to the extent that the course of study is, or is to be, provided wholly or mainly from Australian premises that are related to an overseas higher education award; or
a regulated higher education award; and
the entity is not a registered higher education provider registered in either the “Australian University” or “Overseas University” provider category.
Civil penalty: 600 penalty units.
Use of the word “university”
Without limiting paragraph (1)(a) or (2)(a), an entity is taken to use the word “university” if the entity:
uses a variant of that word; or
uses that word, or a variant of that word, by itself or in combination with other words.

section.heading: Falsely representing entity as a registered higher education provider

content.p: Offence
A regulated entity commits an offence if:
the entity represents that the entity is a registered higher education provider; and
the representation is untrue.
Penalty: 300 penalty units.
Civil penalty
A regulated entity contravenes this subsection if:
the entity represents that the entity is a registered higher education provider; and
the representation is untrue.
Civil penalty: 600 penalty units.

section.heading: Falsely representing that entity provides a course of study leading to a regulated higher education award

content.p: Offence
A regulated entity commits an offence if:
the entity represents that it provides all or part of a course of study that leads to a regulated higher education award; and
the representation is untrue.
Penalty: 120 penalty units.
Civil penalty
A regulated entity contravenes this subsection if:
the entity represents that it provides all or part of a course of study that leads to a regulated higher education award; and
the representation is untrue.
Civil penalty: 240 penalty units.

section.heading: Falsely representing course of study is accredited

content.p: Offence
A regulated entity commits an offence if:
the entity represents that a course of study is an accredited course in relation to an entity; and
the representation is untrue.
Penalty: 120 penalty units.
Civil penalty
A regulated entity contravenes this subsection if:
the entity represents that a course of study is an accredited course in relation to an entity; and
the representation is untrue.
Civil penalty: 240 penalty units.

section.heading: Providing an unaccredited course of study

content.p: Offence
A registered higher education provider commits an offence if:
one or more entities provide all or part of a course of study; and
the course of study leads to a regulated higher education award offered or conferred by the provider; and
the course of study is not an accredited course in relation to the provider.
Penalty: 120 penalty units.
Civil penalty
A registered higher education provider contravenes this subsection if:
one or more entities provide all or part of a course of study; and
the course of study leads to a regulated higher education award offered or conferred by the provider; and
the course of study is not an accredited course in relation to the provider.
Civil penalty: 240 penalty units.
A registered higher education provider contravenes this section if:
a condition is imposed on the provider’s registration; and
the provider does an act or omits to do an act; and
the act or omission breaches the condition.
Civil penalty: 120 penalty units.
A registered higher education provider contravenes this section if:
a condition is imposed on the provider’s authorisation as an authorised offshore provider; and
the provider does an act or omits to do an act; and
the act or omission breaches the condition.
Civil penalty: 120 penalty units.
A registered higher education provider contravenes this section if:
a condition is imposed on the accreditation of a course of study accredited in relation to the provider; and
the provider does an act or omits to do an act; and
the act or omission breaches the condition.
Civil penalty: 120 penalty units.

section.heading: Prohibition on providing etc. academic cheating services

content.p: Providing etc. an academic cheating service for a commercial purpose
A person commits an offence if the person provides, offers to provide or arranges for a third person to provide an academic cheating service:
to a student undertaking, with a higher education provider:
an Australian course of study; or
an overseas course of study provided at Australian premises; and
for a commercial purpose.
Penalty: 2 years imprisonment or 500 penalty units, or both.
Strict liability applies to:
paragraph (1)(a); and
(b) the physical element of circumstance in paragraphs (a) and (b) of the definition of academic cheating service in section 5.
Providing etc. an academic cheating service

A person contravenes this subsection if the person provides, offers to provide or arranges for a third person to provide an academic cheating service to a student undertaking, with a higher education provider:
an Australian course of study; or
an overseas course of study provided at Australian premises.
Civil penalty: 500 penalty units.
Generally not necessary to prove provision etc. of an academic cheating service to a particular student

In proceedings for a contravention of subsection (1) or (3), it is not necessary to prove that the person provided, offered to provide or arranged for a third person to provide an academic cheating service to a particular student.

Subsection (4) does not apply in relation to proceedings for a contravention of subsection (1) or (3) (as that provision is given effect by paragraph 114C(4)(c)) if the student referred to in that subsection is an alien (within the meaning of paragraph 51(xix) of the Constitution).

section.heading: Prohibition on advertising academic cheating services

content.p: A person commits an offence if:
the person advertises, or publishes or broadcasts an advertisement for, an academic cheating service to students undertaking, with a higher education provider:
an Australian course of study; or
an overseas course of study provided at Australian premises; and
either:
the person does so for a commercial purpose; or
the academic cheating service has a commercial purpose.
Penalty: 2 years imprisonment or 500 penalty units, or both.

(2) A person contravenes this subsection if the person advertises, or publishes or broadcasts an advertisement for, an academic cheating service to students undertaking, with a higher education provider:
an Australian course of study; or
an overseas course of study provided at Australian premises.
Civil penalty: 500 penalty units.
In addition to the effect they have in relation to higher education providers, sections 114A and 114B also have effect as provided by this section.
Note: For the meaning of higher education provider, see section 5.
Section 114A—trade and commerce
Section 114A also has the effect it would have as if:

each reference to providing an academic cheating service were expressly confined to a service that is, or is to be, provided in the course of trade and commerce to which paragraph 51(i) of the Constitution applies; or

each reference to an offer to provide, or to an arrangement to provide, an academic cheating service were expressly confined to an offer or arrangement made in the course of trade and commerce to which paragraph 51(i) of the Constitution applies.
Section 114A—communications
Section 114A also has the effect it would have as if:

each reference to providing an academic cheating service were expressly confined to a service that is, or is to be, provided by means of a service to which paragraph 51(v) of the Constitution applies; or

each reference to an offer to provide, or to an arrangement to provide, an academic cheating service were expressly confined to an offer or arrangement made by means of a service to which paragraph 51(v) of the Constitution applies.
Section 114A—aliens
Section 114A also has the effect it would have as if:

each reference to a person who provides, offers to provide or arranges for a third person to provide an academic cheating service were expressly confined to a person who is an alien (within the meaning of paragraph 51(xix) of the Constitution); or
each reference to a third person in respect of whom an arrangement is made were expressly confined to a person who is an alien (within the meaning of paragraph 51(xix) of the Constitution); or
each reference to a student were expressly confined to a person who is an alien (within the meaning of paragraph 51(xix) of the Constitution).
Sections 114A—constitutional corporations (other than higher education providers)
Section 114A also has the effect it would have as if:
each reference to a person who provides, offers to provide or arranges for a third person to provide an academic cheating service were expressly confined to a constitutional corporation; or
each reference to a third person in respect of whom an arrangement is made were expressly confined to a constitutional corporation.
Section 114B—trade and commerce
Section 114B also has the effect it would have as if:

each reference to advertising, or publishing or broadcasting an advertisement for, an academic cheating service were expressly confined to a service that is, or is to be, provided in the course of trade and commerce to which paragraph 51(i) of the Constitution applies; or

each reference to advertising, or publishing or broadcasting an advertisement for, an academic cheating service were expressly confined to advertising, publishing or broadcasting in the course of trade and commerce to which paragraph 51(i) of the Constitution applies.
Section 114B—communications
Section 114B also has the effect it would have as if:

each reference to advertising, or publishing or broadcasting an advertisement for, an academic cheating service were expressly confined to a service that is, or is to be, provided by means of a service to which paragraph 51(v) of the Constitution applies; or

each reference to advertising, or publishing or broadcasting an advertisement for, an academic cheating service were expressly confined to advertising, publishing or broadcasting by means of a service to which paragraph 51(v) of the Constitution applies.
Section 114B—aliens

Section 114B also has the effect it would have as if each reference to a person who advertises, or publishes or broadcasts an advertisement for, an academic cheating service were expressly confined to a person who is an alien (within the meaning of paragraph 51(xix) of the Constitution).
Section 114B—constitutional corporations

Section 114B also has the effect it would have as if each reference to a person who advertises, or publishes or broadcasts an advertisement for, an academic cheating service were expressly confined to a constitutional corporation.
Provisions subject to monitoring
A provision is subject to monitoring under Part 2 of the Regulatory Powers Act if it is:
a provision of this Act; or
a provision of an instrument made under subsection 58(1); or
(c) an offence against the Crimes Act 1914 or the Criminal Code that relates to this Act.
Note: Part 2 of the Regulatory Powers Act creates a framework for monitoring whether this Act has been complied with. It includes powers of entry and inspection.

section.heading: Injunctions relating to online locations that facilitate provision of, or advertising of, academic cheating services

content.p: Application for an injunction

TEQSA may apply, on behalf of the Commonwealth, to the Federal Court to grant an injunction that requires a carriage service provider to take such steps as the Court considers reasonable to disable access to an online location that contravenes, or facilitates a contravention of, section 114A or 114B.

The application under subsection (1) may also request that the injunction require an online search engine provider (other than a provider that is covered by a declaration under subsection (11)) to take such steps as the Court considers reasonable so as not to provide a search result that refers users to the online location.
Granting the injunction
The Court may grant the injunction in the terms, and subject to the conditions, that the Court considers appropriate.
Note 1: For the matters that the Court may take into account when determining whether to grant the injunction, see subsection (7).

Note 2: The terms and conditions of the injunction that apply to a carriage service provider under subsection (1) may be different from those that apply to an online search engine provider under subsection (2).
Without limiting subsection (3), the injunction may:
require the carriage service provider to take reasonable steps to do either or both of the following:
block domain names, URLs and IP addresses that provide access to the online location and that are specified in the injunction;
block domain names, URLs and IP addresses that the carriage service provider and TEQSA agree, in writing, have started to provide access to the online location after the injunction is made; and
require the online search engine provider to take reasonable steps to do either or both of the following:
not provide search results that include domain names, URLs and IP addresses that provide access to the online location and that are specified in the injunction;

not provide search results that include domain names, URLs and IP addresses that the online search engine provider and TEQSA agree, in writing, have started to provide access to the online location after the injunction is made.
Parties
The parties to an action under subsection (1) are:
TEQSA; and
the carriage service provider; and
if the application under subsection (1) also sought for the injunction to apply against an online search engine provider—the online search engine provider; and
the person who operates the online location if, but only if, that person makes an application to be joined as a party to the proceedings.
Service
TEQSA must notify:
the carriage service provider; and
if the application under subsection (1) also sought for the injunction to apply against an online search engine provider—the online search engine provider; and
the person who operates the online location;

of the making of an application under subsection (1), but the Court may dispense, on such terms as it sees fit, with the notice required to be sent under paragraph (c) if the Court is satisfied that TEQSA is unable, despite reasonable efforts, to determine the identity or address of the person who operates the online location, or to send notices to that person.
Matters to be taken into account
In determining whether to grant the injunction, the Court may take the following matters into account:
whether disabling access to the online location is a proportionate response in the circumstances;

if the application under subsection (1) also sought for the injunction to apply against an online search engine provider—whether not providing search results that refer users to the online location is a proportionate response in the circumstances;
the impact on any person, or class of persons, likely to be affected by the grant of the injunction;
whether it is in the public interest to disable access to the online location;

if the application under subsection (1) also sought for the injunction to apply against an online search engine provider—whether it is in the public interest not to provide search results that refer users to the online location;
whether TEQSA complied with subsection (6);
any other remedies available under this Act;
any other matter prescribed by the regulations;
any other relevant matter.
Rescinding and varying injunctions
The Court may:
limit the duration of; or
upon application, rescind or vary;
an injunction granted under this section.
An application under subsection (8) may be made by:
any of the persons referred to in subsection (5); or
any other person prescribed by the regulations.
An application under subsection (8) must not request the Court to vary the injunction so that it applies to an online search engine provider that is covered by a declaration under subsection (11).
Declarations excluding online search engine providers
The Minister may, by legislative instrument, declare that:
a particular online search engine provider; or
an online search engine provider that is a member of a particular class;
must not be specified in an application under subsection (1) or (8).
Costs

A carriage service provider or, if applicable, an online search engine provider is not liable for any costs in relation to the proceedings unless the provider enters an appearance and takes part in the proceedings.
Application of the Regulatory Powers Act

Sections 122 to 125 of the Regulatory Powers Act apply in relation to an application under this section for the grant of an injunction, or to the grant of an injunction under this section, in a corresponding way to the way in which they apply to an application under section 121 of that Act for the grant of an injunction or to the grant of an injunction under section 121 of that Act.

part.heading: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

division.heading: Establishment, functions and powers of TEQSA

content.p: (1) The Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA) is established by this section.
Each State and Territory Minister who is responsible for higher education must be consulted if TEQSA is to be abolished.
(3) For the purposes of the finance law (within the meaning of the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act 2013):
TEQSA is a listed entity; and
the Commissioners are the accountable authority of TEQSA; and
the following persons are officials of TEQSA:
the Commissioners;
the Chief Executive Officer;
the staff of TEQSA referred to in section 156; and
the purposes of TEQSA include the functions of TEQSA referred to in section 134.
TEQSA consists of:
a Chief Commissioner; and
at least one, but not more than 4, other Commissioners.
Note: TEQSA does not have a legal identity separate from the Commonwealth.
TEQSA has the following functions:
to register regulated entities as registered higher education providers in accordance with this Act;
to accredit courses of study in accordance with this Act;
to investigate whether this Act or this Act’s associated provisions have been or are being complied with, including by:
conducting compliance assessments and quality assessments; and
conducting accreditation assessments of accredited courses;
to advise and make recommendations to the Minister on matters relating to the quality or regulation of higher education providers, if requested by the Minister or on its own initiative;
to protect and enhance academic integrity by:
gathering, providing and sharing information, and providing education, in relation to the conduct prohibited by sections 114A and 114B; and
conducting research relating to academic cheating services; and
taking action to prevent access to online sources of academic cheating services;
to collect, analyse, interpret and disseminate information relating to:
higher education providers; and
regulated higher education awards; and
quality assurance practice, and quality improvement, in higher education; and
the Higher Education Standards Framework;
to advise and make recommendations to a higher education provider on matters relating to the Threshold Standards, if requested by the provider in the approved form;
to conduct training to improve the quality of higher education;
to give the Secretary an independent assessment of information the Secretary provides about higher education providers, that uses assessment criteria provided by the Secretary;
to cooperate with its counterparts in other countries;
to develop service standards that TEQSA must meet in performing its functions;
any function determined under subsection (5);
such other functions as are conferred on TEQSA by or under this Act or any other Commonwealth law.
Note: An example for paragraph (m) is TEQSA’s functions under the Education Services for Overseas Students Act 2000.
Without limiting paragraph (1)(m), that paragraph includes a function conferred on TEQSA by an authorisation made for the purposes of a Commonwealth law.
Note: An example would be if the Minister authorised TEQSA to consider whether to consent to a company using “university” in its name for the purposes of section 147 of the Corporations Act 2001.
TEQSA may perform its functions within or outside Australia.
TEQSA has the power to do all things that are necessary or convenient to be done for or in connection with the performance of its functions.
The Minister may, by legislative instrument, determine other functions for TEQSA that relate to higher education.

Subject to section 136 of this Act and section 170C of the Education Services for Overseas Students Act 2000, TEQSA is not subject to direction from anyone in relation to the performance of its functions or the exercise of its powers.

section.heading: Minister may give directions to TEQSA

content.p: The Minister may, by legislative instrument, give directions to TEQSA in relation to the performance of its functions and the exercise of its powers.
Note: Part 4 of Chapter 3 (sunsetting) of the Legislation Act 2003 does not apply to the direction (see regulations made for the purposes of paragraph 54(2)(b) of that Act).
A direction under subsection (1) must be of a general nature only.
Subsection (2) does not apply to a direction that relates to the power conferred by subsection 158(1).
Note: Subsection 158(1) confers a power to determine fees.
(2B) Regulations made for the purposes of paragraph 44(2)(b) of the Legislation Act 2003 do not apply in relation to a direction under subsection (1) of this section.
Note: This means that section 42 (disallowance) of the Legislation Act 2003 applies to the direction.
TEQSA must comply with a direction given under subsection (1).

section.heading: TEQSA has privileges and immunities of the Crown

content.p: TEQSA has the privileges and immunities of the Crown in right of the Commonwealth.
Each Commissioner is to be appointed by the Minister by written instrument.
A Commissioner may hold office on either a full-time or a part-time basis.
A person may only be appointed as a Commissioner if the Minister is satisfied that the person has appropriate qualifications, knowledge or experience.
Note: A Commissioner is eligible for reappointment: see section 33AA of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901.
A Commissioner holds office for the period specified in the instrument of appointment. The period must not exceed 5 years.

A Commissioner is to be paid the remuneration that is determined by the Remuneration Tribunal. If no determination of that remuneration by the Tribunal is in operation, the Commissioner is to be paid the remuneration that is determined, in writing, by the Minister.
A Commissioner is to be paid the allowances that are determined, in writing, by the Minister.
(3) This section has effect subject to the Remuneration Tribunal Act 1973.
A full-time Commissioner has the recreation leave entitlements that are determined by the Remuneration Tribunal.
The Minister may grant a full-time Commissioner leave of absence, other than recreation leave, on the terms and conditions as to remuneration or otherwise that the Minister determines.
The Chief Commissioner may grant leave of absence to a part-time Commissioner (other than the Chief Commissioner) on the terms and conditions that the Chief Commissioner determines.
If the Chief Commissioner is a part-time Commissioner, the Minister may grant leave of absence to the Chief Commissioner on the terms and conditions that the Minister determines.
A full-time Commissioner must not engage in paid employment outside the duties of his or her office without the Minister’s approval.
A part-time Commissioner must not engage in any paid employment that, in the Minister’s opinion, conflicts or may conflict with the proper performance of his or her duties.

section.heading: Disclosure of interests to the Minister

content.p: A Commissioner must give written notice to the Minister of all interests, pecuniary or otherwise, that the Commissioner has or acquires that conflict or could conflict with the proper performance of the Commissioner’s functions.
The notice must be given to the Minister as soon as practicable after the Commissioner becomes aware of the potential for conflict of interest.
A Commissioner holds office on the terms and conditions (if any) in relation to matters not covered by this Act that are determined, in writing, by the Minister.
A Commissioner may resign his or her appointment by giving the Minister a written resignation.
The resignation takes effect on the day it is received by the Minister or, if a later day is specified in the resignation, on that later day.
The Minister may terminate the appointment of a Commissioner:
for misbehaviour; or
if the Commissioner is unable to perform the duties of his or her office because of physical or mental incapacity.
The Minister may terminate the appointment of a Commissioner if:
the Commissioner:
becomes bankrupt; or
takes steps to take the benefit of any law for the relief of bankrupt or insolvent debtors; or
compounds with one or more of his or her creditors; or
makes an assignment of his or her remuneration for the benefit of one or more of his or her creditors; or
the Commissioner is a full-time Commissioner and is absent, except on leave of absence, for 14 consecutive days or for 30 days in any 12 months; or
the Commissioner is a part-time Commissioner and is absent, except on leave of absence, from 3 consecutive TEQSA meetings; or
the Commissioner engages in paid employment contrary to section 142; or
the Commissioner fails, without reasonable excuse, to comply with section 143 or 150.
The Minister must terminate the appointment of a Commissioner if the Commissioner becomes an executive officer of a higher education provider.
Acting Chief Commissioner
The Minister may, by written instrument, appoint a Commissioner to act as the Chief Commissioner:
during a vacancy in the office of the Chief Commissioner (whether or not an appointment has previously been made to the office); or
during any period, or during all periods, when the Chief Commissioner:
is absent from duty or from Australia; or
is, for any reason, unable to perform the duties of the office.
Acting Commissioner
The Minister may, by written instrument, appoint a person to act as a Commissioner (other than the Chief Commissioner):
during a vacancy in the office of the Commissioner (whether or not an appointment has previously been made to the office); or
during any period, or during all periods, when the Commissioner:
is absent from duty or from Australia; or
is, for any reason, unable to perform the duties of the office.
Requirements before appointing a person to act
A person may only be appointed to act as the Chief Commissioner, or as a Commissioner, if the Minister is satisfied that the person has appropriate qualifications, knowledge or experience.
Note: For rules that apply to acting appointments, see sections 33AB and 33A of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901.
Subdivision A—Meetings
The Chief Commissioner must ensure that such meetings are held as are necessary for the efficient performance of TEQSA’s functions.
Meetings are to be held at such times and places as the Chief Commissioner decides.
The Chief Commissioner must convene a meeting if requested, in writing, by at least 2 of the other Commissioners.
Presiding at meetings
The Chief Commissioner presides at all meetings at which he or she is present.
If the Chief Commissioner is not present at a meeting, a Commissioner:
nominated by the Chief Commissioner; and
present at the meeting;
must preside.
Quorum
At a meeting of TEQSA, a quorum is constituted by a majority of Commissioners.
Rules of procedure
TEQSA may, subject to this Division, regulate proceedings at its meetings as it considers appropriate.
Note: Section 33B of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 provides for participation in meetings by telephone etc.
Voting
The person presiding at a meeting of TEQSA has a deliberative vote but, if the votes are equal, does not have a casting vote.
Minutes
TEQSA must ensure that minutes of its meetings are kept.

If a Commissioner has an interest, pecuniary or otherwise, in a matter being considered, or about to be considered, at a meeting, the Commissioner must disclose the nature of that interest to the other Commissioners.
The disclosure must be made as soon as possible after the relevant facts have come to the Commissioner’s knowledge.
The disclosure must be recorded in the minutes of the meeting.
Unless TEQSA otherwise determines, the Commissioner:
must not be present during TEQSA’s deliberation on the matter; and
must not take part in TEQSA’s decision on the matter.
For the purposes of TEQSA making a determination under subsection (4), the Commissioner:
must not be present during any of TEQSA’s deliberations for the purpose of making the determination; and
must not take part in making the determination.
A determination under subsection (4) must be recorded in the minutes of the meeting.
Subdivision B—Decisions without meetings
A decision is taken to have been made at a meeting of TEQSA if:
without meeting, a majority of Commissioners indicate agreement with the proposed decision in accordance with the method determined by TEQSA under subsection (2); and
all Commissioners were informed of the proposed decision, or reasonable efforts were made to inform all Commissioners of the proposed decision.
Subsection (1) applies if TEQSA:
has determined that it applies; and
has determined the method by which Commissioners are to indicate agreement with proposed decisions.
TEQSA must keep a record of decisions made in accordance with section 151.
Subdivision A—Office and functions of the Chief Executive Officer
There is to be a Chief Executive Officer of TEQSA.

section.heading: Functions and powers of the Chief Executive Officer

content.p: The Chief Executive Officer is responsible for the management and administration of TEQSA.
All acts and things done in the name of, or on behalf of, TEQSA by the Chief Executive Officer are taken to have been done by TEQSA.
Subdivision B—Appointment of the Chief Executive Officer

during any period, or during all periods, when the Chief Executive Officer:
is absent from duty or from Australia; or
is, for any reason, unable to perform the duties of the office.

(3) This section has effect subject to the Remuneration Tribunal Act 1973.

The Chief Executive Officer must not engage in paid employment outside the duties of his or her office without the Minister’s approval.

section.heading: Disclosure of interests to the Minister

content.p: The Chief Executive Officer must give written notice to the Minister of all interests, pecuniary or otherwise, that the Chief Executive Officer has or acquires and that conflict or could conflict with the proper performance of the Chief Executive Officer’s functions.
The Chief Executive Officer may resign his or her appointment by giving the Minister a written resignation.

for misbehaviour; or
if the Chief Executive Officer is unable to perform the duties of his or her office because of physical or mental incapacity.

the Chief Executive Officer:
becomes bankrupt; or
takes steps to take the benefit of any law for the relief of bankrupt or insolvent debtors; or
compounds with one or more of his or her creditors; or
makes an assignment of his or her remuneration for the benefit of one or more of his or her creditors; or
the Chief Executive Officer is absent, except on leave of absence, for 14 consecutive days or for 30 days in any 12 months; or
the Chief Executive Officer engages in paid employment contrary to section 154F; or
the Chief Executive Officer fails, without reasonable excuse, to comply with section 154G.
The Chief Executive Officer holds office on the terms and conditions (if any) in relation to matters not covered by this Act that are determined by the Minister.
Subdivision D—Delegation

section.heading: Delegation by the Chief Executive Officer

content.p: The Chief Executive Officer may, by writing, delegate any or all of his or her functions and powers under this Act to a member of the staff of TEQSA who holds:
the classification of APS Executive Level 1 or higher; or
an equivalent classification.

The Chief Executive Officer may, in writing, delegate the Chief Executive Officer’s powers and functions under the Regulatory Powers Act as it applies in relation to this Act, to a member of the staff of TEQSA who is:
an SES employee or an acting SES employee; or
an APS employee who holds or performs the duties of an Executive Level 1 or 2 position or an equivalent position.
Before delegating a function or power under subsection (1) or (2), the Chief Executive Officer must have regard to:

if the function or power is delegated to an APS employee holding, occupying, or performing the duties of, a specified office or position—whether the office or position is sufficiently senior for the employee to perform the function or exercise the power; or
otherwise—whether the employee has appropriate qualifications or expertise to perform the function or duty or exercise the power.
A delegate must comply with any written directions of the Chief Executive Officer.
Subdivision E—Directions by Minister

section.heading: Minister may give directions to Chief Executive Officer

content.p: The Minister may, by legislative instrument, give written directions to the Chief Executive Officer about the performance of his or her functions and the exercise of his or her powers.
Note: Part 4 of Chapter 3 (sunsetting) of the Legislation Act 2003 does not apply to the direction (see regulations made for the purposes of paragraph 54(2)(b) of that Act).
(1A) Regulations made for the purposes of paragraph 44(2)(b) of the Legislation Act 2003 do not apply in relation to a direction under subsection (1) of this section.
Note: This means that section 42 (disallowance) of the Legislation Act 2003 applies to the direction.
The Chief Executive Officer must comply with a direction under subsection (1).

(3) Subsection (2) does not apply to the extent that the direction relates to the Chief Executive Officer’s performance of functions, or exercise of powers, under the Public Service Act 1999 in relation to TEQSA.
Subdivision F—Other matters

section.heading: Chief Executive Officer not subject to direction by TEQSA on certain matters

content.p: To avoid doubt, the Chief Executive Officer is not subject to direction by TEQSA in relation to the Chief Executive Officer’s performance of functions, or exercise of powers, under:
(a) the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act 2013; or
(b) the Public Service Act 1999;
in relation to TEQSA.
(1) The staff of TEQSA are to be persons engaged under the Public Service Act 1999.
(2) For the purposes of the Public Service Act 1999:
the Chief Executive Officer and the staff of TEQSA together constitute a Statutory Agency; and
the Chief Executive Officer is the Head of that Statutory Agency.

section.heading: Staff to be made available to TEQSA

content.p: TEQSA is to be assisted by:
officers and employees of Commonwealth authorities whose services are made available to TEQSA in connection with the performance of TEQSA’s functions or the exercise of its powers; and
persons whose services are made available under arrangements made under subsection (2).

The Chief Executive Officer may arrange for officers or employees of an appropriate State or Territory authority to be made available to TEQSA to perform services in connection with the performance of TEQSA’s functions or the exercise of its powers.
An arrangement under subsection (2) may provide for the Commonwealth to reimburse a State or Territory with respect to the services of a person to whom the arrangement relates.
When performing services for TEQSA under this section, a person is subject to the directions of the Chief Executive Officer.
TEQSA may, by legislative instrument, determine fees that TEQSA may charge for things done in the performance of its functions.
TEQSA may, in the determination under subsection (1), determine the way in which a fee is to be worked out.
TEQSA may, in the determination under subsection (1), determine other matters relating to the payment of fees, including:
the circumstances in which fees may be paid in instalments; and
the circumstances in which fees may be set off against another amount payable; and
the circumstances in which fees may be waived.
The fees determined under subsection (1) must not be such as to amount to taxation.
Ministerial approval
TEQSA must not make an instrument under subsection (1) unless the Minister has given written approval to the making of the instrument.
TEQSA must give the Minister such information as the Minister reasonably requires for the purposes of making a decision under subsection (5).
(1) The Commissioners must give a copy of a corporate plan prepared under section 35 of the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act 2013 to the Minister for approval before:
30 April before the first reporting period to which the plan relates; or
such later day as the Minister allows.
Subsection (1) does not apply to a corporate plan if the Minister decides the plan does not need approval.
A corporate plan comes into force on:
if the plan needs Ministerial approval—the later of:
the day it is approved by the Minister; and
the first day of the period to which it relates; or
otherwise—the first day of the period to which it relates.
Varying plans with Ministerial approval
(1) The Commissioners may, with the Minister’s approval, vary a corporate plan prepared under section 35 of the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act 2013.
The Minister may, at any time, request the Commissioners to vary the corporate plan. The Commissioners must comply with the request.
A variation approved by the Minister takes effect on the day it is approved.
Ministerial approval not required for minor variations
Despite subsection (1), the Commissioners may vary the corporate plan without the approval of the Minister if the variation is of a minor nature. The variation takes effect on the day it is made.
If the Commissioners make a variation of a minor nature, the Commissioners must inform the Minister of the variation as soon as is practicable.

Note 2: Reviewable decisions not made by delegates may be reviewed by the Administrative Review Tribunal (see section 187).

section.heading: Applying for internal review of reviewable decisions made by delegates of TEQSA

content.p: This section applies to a reviewable decision if the decision is made by a delegate of TEQSA.
A person affected by a reviewable decision who is dissatisfied with the decision may apply to TEQSA for TEQSA to review the decision.
The application must:
be in the approved form; and
set out the reasons for the application; and
be accompanied by the fee (if any) determined under section 158 for a review under section 185.
Note: The approved form could, for example, require verification by statutory declaration of certain statements.
The application must be made within:
30 days after the applicant is informed of the decision; or
such longer period as TEQSA allows.
Upon receiving an application under section 184, TEQSA must review the reviewable decision.
TEQSA may:
affirm, vary or revoke the reviewable decision; and
if TEQSA revokes the decision, make such other decision as TEQSA thinks appropriate.
TEQSA’s review must be done by:
if the reviewable decision was made by a delegate who was a member of the staff of TEQSA—another delegate who:
is a Commissioner; or
occupies a position senior to that occupied by the first-mentioned delegate; and
otherwise—TEQSA.
TEQSA’s decision on review has effect (except for the purposes of section 183) as if it were made under the provision under which the reviewable decision was made.
TEQSA must, within 30 days of making its decision on review, notify the applicant, in writing, of:
the decision; and
the reasons for the decision.
TEQSA must make its decision on review of a reviewable decision within 90 days after receiving the application for review.

TEQSA is taken, for the purposes of this Part, to have made a decision under subsection 185(2) affirming the reviewable decision if it has not notified the applicant of its decision on review before the end of that 90-day period.

section.heading: Review by the Administrative Review Tribunal

content.p: An application may be made to the Administrative Review Tribunal for review of:
a reviewable decision if the decision was not made by a delegate of TEQSA; or
a decision of TEQSA under subsection 185(2).
Subdivision B—Review of tuition protection decisions

If:
